'''''Oenothera glazioviana''''' is a species of flowering plant in the [[Onagraceae|evening primrose family]] known by the common names '''large-flowered evening-primrose'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> and '''redsepal evening primrose'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=OEGL|taxon=Oenothera glazioviana|accessdate=29 January 2016}}</ref> '''''Oenothera lamarckiana''''' was formerly believed to be a distinct species, but is now regarded as a synonym of ''Oe. glazioviana''. ''Oenothera glazioviana'' can be found in scattered locations worldwide as an [[introduced species]] and in some locations behaves as an [[invasive species]]. It has long been cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]].

==Description==
''Oenothera glazioviana'' is generally a biennial herb producing an erect stem approaching {{convert|1.5|m|ft}} in maximum height. It is roughly hairy in texture, the hairs with reddish blistering or glandular bases. The crinkly leaves are up to 15 centimeters long.

The [[inflorescence]] is a showy spike of many large flowers. When in bud the long red [[sepal]]s are visible. When in bloom each flower has four bright yellow petals up to 5 centimeters long which fade orange to red with age. The fruit is a lance-shaped capsule 2 or 3 centimeters long.

==Taxonomy==
''Oenothera glazioviana'' was first described by [[Marc Micheli]] in 1875.<ref name="IPNI_317809-2">{{cite web |title=''Oenothera glazioviana'' Micheli |work=[[International Plant Names Index|The International Plant Names Index]] |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/317809-2 |access-date=2021-08-22 }}</ref> This species is of hybrid origin from a cross between two North American species, ''[[Oenothera elata]]'' and ''[[Oenothera grandiflora]]'' in Europe.<ref name=POWO_317809-2>{{cite web |title=''Oenothera glazioviana'' Micheli |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:317809-2 |access-date=2025-11-25 }}</ref><ref name="FNA"/> It was soon introduced to the horticultural trade and spread rapidly around the world.<ref name="FNA">{{Cite web|author=Wagner, Warren L. |website=Flora of North America North of Mexico |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York, Oxford |title=Oenothera glazioviana|url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Oenothera_glazioviana|access-date= 25 November 2025}}</ref>

===''Oenothera lamarckiana''===
About a century ago, it was believed that there was a different species, either native to some obscure and unknown place in North America, from which it had quickly spread across the world, or more likely a new species which had very recently evolved in the last few decades, possibly in Europe from a hybrid of two other species, and thence had become a common weed. These theories stemmed from the fact that although the species was now a common species, and while an obviously striking species unlikely to be overlooked by botanists, it had only been recorded in recent times, and never in a truly wild state. [[Oenothera#Genetics|At the time]] this [[taxon]] was important for the brand new study of [[genetics]], the debate about the cause of evolution, whether that was [[natural selection]] or [[Alternatives to Darwinism|one of the alternatives]] such as [[mutationism]], and particularly to the discovery of [[polyploidy]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=de Vries |first=Hugo |author-link=Hugo de Vries |date=January 1918 |title=Mutations of ''Oenothera suaveolens'' Desf. |journal=Genetics |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=1–26 |doi=10.1093/genetics/3.1.1 |pmid=17245896 |pmc=1199547 |url=https://www.genetics.org/content/genetics/3/1/1.full.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=de Vries |first=Hugo |author-link=Hugo de Vries |date=January 1919 |title=''Oenothera rubrinervis''; A Half Mutant |journal=Botanical Gazette |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=1–26 |jstor=2468868 |doi=10.1086/332396|s2cid=83752035 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431405 }}</ref><ref>{{citation |author=Darlington, C. D. |year=1931 |title=Meiosis |journal=Biological Reviews |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=221–264 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-185X.1931.tb01027.x|s2cid=221528298 }}</ref><ref>Cleland R. E. (1962): The cytogenetics of ''Oenothera''. Advance. Genet 11: 147.</ref> It was later discovered that it had, in fact, already been discovered and [[Species description|described]] by a botanist in Brazil only a few decades beforehand, in 1875, as ''Oenothera glazioviana'', and had likely spread across the world from there since then, but this had apparently somehow been overlooked.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:317809-2 |title=''Oenothera glazioviana'' Micheli |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Board of Trustees of the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |access-date=17 August 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Oenothera glazioviana'' arose as a garden hybrid between ''[[Oenothera elata]]'' and ''[[Oenothera grandiflora]]'' in Europe.<ref name=POWO_317809-2/> It is cultivated as an ornamental plant,<ref>{{Citation |title=Oenothera glazioviana |website=Plants |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/159009/Oenothera-glazioviana/Details |access-date=2021-08-22 }}</ref> and has become naturalized in many countries around the world,<ref name=POWO_317809-2/> like Britain and Ireland, where it is the most common species of its genus.<ref name=OABIF>{{Citation |title=Oenothera glazioviana |journal=Systematic Botany Monographs |year=1997 |volume=50 |pages=1–234 |publisher=Biological Records Centre |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/oenothera-glazioviana |access-date=2021-08-22 |archive-date=2021-08-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210822124351/https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/oenothera-glazioviana |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Ecology== 
Under the synonym ''Oenothera lamarckiana'', it is described as a very adaptable plant: however it needs full sun, average moisture, and well-drained [[soil]]s. It is easily grown from seed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.americanmeadows.com/wildflower-seeds/wildflower-species/evening-primrose-seeds|title=Evening Primrose Seeds - American Meadows|publisher=|access-date=2021-08-22|archive-date=2016-11-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161110223942/http://www.americanmeadows.com/wildflower-seeds/wildflower-species/evening-primrose-seeds|url-status=dead}}</ref> It began being grown in European gardens during the 1800s. <ref> {{cite book |last= Endersby |first= Jim |date= 2007|title= A Guinea Pig's History of Biology|location= London|publisher= Harvard University Press |page=130 |isbn=9780674027138}} </ref>
